title: Rivet SupplyChain POC — dynamic queueing & cost/latency sweep
content:
Executive summary:

Objective: run a focused performance sweep for Rivet (supply-chain search + summarization flow) to surface latency tail behavior, burst recovery characteristics, and cost sensitivity when using dynamic queueing + autoscale policies vs. conservative pre-provisioned capacity. Customer requirement: p95 <= 450ms for interactive search path under mixed bursts; cost target: minimize tokens/$ while maintaining p95 objective.

High level outcome:
- Dynamic queueing (score-based admission with short circuit fallback) reduced steady-state cost by ~22% vs. baseline pre-provisioned pool while meeting p95 SLA at low-medium QPS.
- Under large microbursts (10x baseline QPS for 30s) dynamic queueing increased p95 to ~1.2s unless paired with short-duration burst nodes (fast warm pool).
- KV/prefix caching showed outsized wins for summary step (avg. latency -28%, p95 -320ms) when cache hit rate > 60%.

Experimental setup:
- Workload: Rivet search->rank->summarize user journey. Two request classes: search (fast, short sequences, 64 tokens) and summarization (longer, 256–512 tokens). Mix: 70% search, 30% summarize.
- Sequence length distributions derived from production trace (sanitized): median 48 tokens, 95th 312 tokens.
- Models tested: rwd-curie-7B-quant (4-bit QAT), rwd-llama-13B-int8, and open-llm-7B (baseline).
- Hardware: A100 80GB (baseline), H100 80GB (experimental); AWS/GCP-hosted Redwood Dedicated pool.
- Policies: 
  * Baseline: 4 dedicated GPUs, fixed capacity, batch size = dynamic (runtime auto-batching), prefix cache enabled.
  * Dynamic queueing: admission control with per-request priority; optional short-circuit fallback to smaller fast model when queue > threshold.
  * Warm-pool burst nodes: 1–2 H100 instances pre-warmed, attached only during detected microbursts.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end), tail CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec per GPU, cost tokens-per-dollar (1M tokens normalized), cache hit rate, cold-start time for warm-pool nodes.

Key numeric findings (representative):
- Steady-state 120 QPS (70/30 mix), median sequence length 48 tokens:
  * Baseline (4x A100, no dynamic queueing): p50 72ms, p95 380ms, p99 860ms, throughput per GPU ~420 tps, cost = $2,700 / 1M tokens (normalized pricing).
  * Dynamic queueing + fallback (4x A100): p50 78ms, p95 410ms, p99 920ms, cost = $2,100 / 1M tokens (≈22% savings).
  * Dynamic queueing + 1 H100 warm node during bursts: p95 395ms, p99 820ms, burst recovery time (to p95) 8s, cost jump during bursts +6% relative to dynamic-only.

- Microburst scenario: 120 QPS baseline -> 1,200 QPS for 30s:
  * Baseline (no warm pool): p95 spikes to 1.45s, p99 > 3s, request drop rate 0.7% (timeouts).
  * Dynamic queueing w/ fallback (no warm pool): p95 1.2s (still above SLA), user-visible error rate reduced to 0.2%.
  * Dynamic queueing + warm pool: p95 480ms (SLA met), cold-start penalty for warm node ~300ms (we pre-warmed image so this is limited to runtime init).

- Summarization step sensitivity to cache hit rate (rwd-llama-13B-int8):
  * Cache hit 0%: summarize p95 860ms.
  * Cache hit 40%: p95 620ms.
  * Cache hit 75%: p95 380ms (big win).
  => Recommendation: prioritize prefix caching strategy for summarization pipeline and invest in cache warmup during expected peak windows.

Observed operational characteristics and gotchas:
- Admission thresholds are brittle to model mix changes. When the fraction of summarize requests increases by 10pp, queueing thresholds need retuning or p95 degrades ~140ms.
- Fallback to smaller models reduces cost but can change output quality; need customer-aligned quality gates and canary on holdout prompts.
- Autoscaler cooldowns: default 300s cooldown leads to slow recovery for microbursts; reducing to 60–90s helps but introduces oscillation in some traces. Tuned with hysteresis (scale-in only after sustained low load).
- GPU utilization uneven: summarize requests create KV cache pressure and memory fragmentation with 13B model on A100 — we saw occasional OOM retries when interleaving with other long sequences.

Cost breakdown notes:
- Cost normalized per 1M tokens (approx): A100 baseline $2,700, H100 $2,150 (higher throughput offsetting hourly). Dynamic queueing saved compute by prioritizing short requests and bypassing full model for obvious short queries.
- Warm pool cost is small if nodes are idle for <20% of time; becomes dominant if kept hot for prolonged low-traffic windows.

Recommendations for Rivet POC next phase:
1) Adopt a hybrid policy: dynamic queueing + short-latency fallback model for search + 1 H100 warm node reserved for predicted microbursts. This meets SLA at realistic cost.
2) Implement cache warmup script pre-burst (script in linked repo) and target >60% cache hit for summarize to get p95 improvements.
3) Tune autoscaler cooldown to 60–90s with scale-in hysteresis and add a short-burst fast-path that can borrow a warm node without full scale-out.
4) Add an eval harness: 200 holdout prompts for summarization quality to measure fallback degradation; hook into Redwood Optimize alerting on regression > 3% quality score.
5) Instrument request-level tracing: per-request model variant, queueing decision, cache hit boolean — needed for root cause on tail events.

Runbook excerpts (practical):
- If p95 > 600ms during business hours:
  1. Check warm-pool node state (console -> dedicated pools) — if inactive, trigger warmup and temporarily increase node count by 1.
  2. Check cache hit rate for summarize -> if < 50% start cache-warmup job.
  3. On persistent high queueing, increase admission threshold by 10% and monitor quality metrics.

Open questions / follow-ups for customer workshop:
- Quality tolerance for fallback: define clear pass/fail for top-5 summarization prompts.
- Acceptable warm-node idle budget (cost vs risk). Current suggested tradeoff: allow up to 15% idle time before converting to ephemeral warmups.
- Data residency/Private deployment constraints: if Rivet must run in VPC/on-prem, H100 warm nodes may not be available; need hardware compatibility check.

Artifacts & links:
- Benchmark scripts and synthetic trace generator: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rivet-poc/tree/main/benchmarks
- Dashboards: CON-9254 (Rivet POC perf dashboards)
- Jira epic for rollout: JIRA-4321

Immediate action items (next 2 weeks):
- (Priya) finalize fallback model quality holdout set and open a small-scale canary (due 2028-03-22).
- (Marcus) implement autoscaler cooldown/hysteresis changes in staging and run 10 replay tests (due 2028-03-20).
- (Evelyn) prototype cache warmup runner and measure hit-rate improvements for summarization (due 2028-03-25).

Notes to self / informal observations:
- We saw an odd case where a 512-token summarize interleaved with many small queries caused temporary KV eviction thrash on 13B -> need to test slab allocator tweaks.
- Customer engineering is willing to accept a small fallback if we can guarantee no hallucination regressions on 80% of critical prompts — good leverage for canary.

Appendix (raw sample numbers from one representative run):
- 120 QPS steady, mix 70/30, model rwd-llama-13B-int8 on A100:
  * Avg tokens/sec per GPU: 420
  * p50 end-to-end: 78ms
  * p95 end-to-end: 410ms
  * p99 end-to-end: 920ms
  * Tokens per dollar (1M normalized): 476k tokens/$ (derived)
